questions.q: How does the article define “a true man”?
options: One who is good outwardly, whatever lies within
Not quite. The article says: One whose inner personality is better than his outward one, with no double standard.
One who impresses others with charm and wit
Not quite. The article says: One whose inner personality is better than his outward one, with no double standard.
One who hides his faults well
Not quite. The article says: One whose inner personality is better than his outward one, with no double standard.
One whose inner personality is better than his outward one, with no double standard
Yes. The religious name for a double standard is hypocrisy.
questions.rationale: “A true man is one whose inner personality is better than his outward personality. He should not be a person with double standards.”

questions.q: Reflecting on an article headed “Win the War; Lose the Peace,” what does the diary say wars do to the problems they are meant to solve?
options: They make them disappear with time
Not quite. The article says: They create even more problems, for victor and vanquished alike.
They settle them for a generation
Not quite. The article says: They create even more problems, for victor and vanquished alike.
They create even more problems, for victor and vanquished alike
Right. “Problems are created by problem-solving activity.”
They solve them for the winning side
Not quite. The article says: They create even more problems, for victor and vanquished alike.
questions.rationale: “They are all fought to find a solution to some problem. But every war in turn has created even more problems.”

questions.q: What does the diary say set the Prophet apart in confrontational situations?
options: He used peace as his means, and chose battle hardly at all
Yes. Peace is described as the strongest force.
He always had the larger force
Not quite. The article says: He used peace as his means, and chose battle hardly at all.
He avoided all contact with opponents
Not quite. The article says: He used peace as his means, and chose battle hardly at all.
He relied on allies to fight for him
Not quite. The article says: He used peace as his means, and chose battle hardly at all.
questions.rationale: “The number of times he actually chose to go to war was almost negligible… the Prophet used peace as his weapon.”

questions.q: Visitors fell silent and reverent on entering a presidential palace. What contrast did this suggest to the writer?
options: People show awe in a human palace, yet walk through God’s world – a far greater palace – with indifference
Well read. He calls for humility and awe.
Presidents deserve less respect than kings
Not quite. The article says: People show awe in a human palace, yet walk through God’s world – a far greater palace – with indifference.
Palaces are wasteful and should be closed
Not quite. The article says: People show awe in a human palace, yet walk through God’s world – a far greater palace – with indifference.
Conferences ought to be held outdoors
Not quite. The article says: People show awe in a human palace, yet walk through God’s world – a far greater palace – with indifference.
questions.rationale: “In the world of God, people walk with an indifference that contrasts sharply with the reverence they exhibit while traversing the corridors of human palaces.”

questions.q: How does the article describe death?
options: As a punishment for wrongdoing
Not quite. The article says: As a transition from one place to another in an unbroken life, not the end of it.
As a transition from one place to another in an unbroken life, not the end of it
Correct. A “period of transition.”
As the end of a person’s existence
Not quite. The article says: As a transition from one place to another in an unbroken life, not the end of it.
As a pause before life on earth resumes
Not quite. The article says: As a transition from one place to another in an unbroken life, not the end of it.
questions.rationale: “It signifies a transfer from one place to another, rather than the end of life.”

questions.q: What principle about responsibility does the article draw from the verse “God does not impose responsibility on anyone except according to his strength”?
options: Every duty falls equally on every person
Not quite. The article says: Duty depends on capacity – no one is answerable for what lies beyond his means.
Only scholars carry religious duties
Not quite. The article says: Duty depends on capacity – no one is answerable for what lies beyond his means.
Duties may be set aside whenever inconvenient
Not quite. The article says: Duty depends on capacity – no one is answerable for what lies beyond his means.
Duty depends on capacity – no one is answerable for what lies beyond his means
Yes. The more one is able, the more is asked.
questions.rationale: “Responsibility in God’s religion is contingent on one’s capability… they are not accountable for matters beyond their control.”

questions.q: How does the article sum up the difference between personal and collective matters?
options: “No standard for either”
Not quite. The article says: “Idealism at the individual level, pragmatism at the social level”.
“Idealism at the individual level, pragmatism at the social level”
Right. Society needs consensus; imposing an approach breeds conflict.
“The same strict standard for both”
Not quite. The article says: “Idealism at the individual level, pragmatism at the social level”.
“Pragmatism for oneself, idealism for society”
Not quite. The article says: “Idealism at the individual level, pragmatism at the social level”.
questions.rationale: “The solution lies in distinguishing between individual quality and collective feasibility… ‘Idealism at the individual level, pragmatism at the social level.’”

questions.q: Why, according to the article, would a society in which everyone held identical views stagnate?
options: Minds develop through the meeting of different ideas; without it, growth is stunted
Yes. Diversity of opinion is a blessing.
It would have too many leaders
Not quite. The article says: Minds develop through the meeting of different ideas; without it, growth is stunted.
It would grow too quickly
Not quite. The article says: Minds develop through the meeting of different ideas; without it, growth is stunted.
It would quarrel over small things
Not quite. The article says: Minds develop through the meeting of different ideas; without it, growth is stunted.
questions.rationale: “Personal evolution takes place only where the interaction of divergent thinking provides the requisite mental stimuli.”

questions.q: What does the article call the starting point of religion, drawn from the opening verse of the Quran?
options: Joining a community
Not quite. The article says: Recognition and understanding of God, the Lord of all – before rules and regulations.
Memorising without understanding
Not quite. The article says: Recognition and understanding of God, the Lord of all – before rules and regulations.
Learning the detailed rules first
Not quite. The article says: Recognition and understanding of God, the Lord of all – before rules and regulations.
Recognition and understanding of God, the Lord of all – before rules and regulations
Exactly. The right sequence builds sincere faith.
questions.rationale: “It marks the fundamental point of departure in matters of faith—the acknowledgment of God, the Sovereign of all realms.”

questions.q: What does the article describe as Gandhiji’s unfulfilled mission, and how can it be carried forward?
options: Political independence – by mass protest
Not quite. The article says: Social change through non-violence – by educating individual minds in tolerance and avoidance.
Industrial growth – by new laws
Not quite. The article says: Social change through non-violence – by educating individual minds in tolerance and avoidance.
Social change through non-violence – by educating individual minds in tolerance and avoidance
Well read. Violence begins, and can end, in the mind.
A larger army – by recruitment
Not quite. The article says: Social change through non-violence – by educating individual minds in tolerance and avoidance.
questions.rationale: “Mahatma Gandhi also wanted to herald social change in India on the basis of non violence… there is only one way… to bring about a change in the thinking of the individual.”
